title: Three-Property Rule Strategy
name: Three-Property Rule Strategy
metaTitle: Three-Property Rule Strategy in Philadelphia, PA
metaDescription: Deciding when naming just three Philadelphia candidates, regardless of combined value, is the sharper identification path before the 45-day deadline.

sections.html: The three-property rule lets an exchanger name up to three replacement candidates with no cap on their combined value, which is the simplest of the identification rules on paper but the least forgiving in practice, since naming exactly three properties means every one of them has to actually be capable of closing. We use it deliberately, not by default, and only after the pipeline has produced three candidates strong enough to carry that concentration.

sections.heading: When Three Names Is the Right Call
sections.html: The rule fits an exchanger who has found a genuinely strong lead, a well-located medical office near University City or a clean industrial parcel along the port corridor, and wants to name it alongside two credible backups without worrying about a combined value ceiling the way the 200 percent rule imposes. It works less well for an exchanger still casting a wide net, since naming only three candidates in a market with this much competing capital can mean all three are gone by day 45 if the pipeline wasn't deep enough behind them.

sections.heading: Why Value Doesn't Matter Under This Rule
sections.html:
Unlike the 200 percent rule, the three-property rule places no limit on how much the three named candidates are worth combined, which means an exchanger can name one large trophy asset alongside two much smaller backups without doing any value math at all. That flexibility is useful when the strongest candidate is disproportionately larger than the relinquished property's sale price, a scenario where the 200 percent rule's value cap could otherwise force an uncomfortable choice.

An exchanger selling a modest Philadelphia rowhouse portfolio and eyeing a single larger industrial asset near the port, for example, could easily find that one candidate alone exceeds 200 percent of the sale price, which makes the three-property rule the only workable path if that asset stays the top choice.

sections.heading: The Concentration Risk This Rule Creates
sections.html:
Naming only three properties means there's no room to add a fourth candidate later if all three run into trouble, no financing falls through on one, title issues surface on another, so the three names have to be selected with real conviction, not as placeholders while sourcing continues.

  • Confirm each of the three candidates has cleared preliminary title and use review before naming it
  • Verify financing feasibility on every candidate rather than only the strongest one
  • Check that at least one candidate isn't already competing against another active offer from a different buyer
  • Weigh whether the 200 percent rule might fit better if a fourth strong candidate exists but value stays under the cap
  • Confirm the written identification is filed with unambiguous property descriptions for all three

The exchanger's own risk tolerance matters here too, since some would rather carry the concentration of three strong names than the added complexity of tracking a longer list under the 200 percent rule, even when both paths are technically available.

sections.heading: Comparing It Against the Alternative Rules
sections.html:
An exchanger with four or more real candidates whose combined value stays under twice the relinquished sale price is often better served by the 200 percent rule, since that path doesn't force dropping a viable fourth or fifth option down to three. The three-property rule earns its place when the pipeline has narrowed naturally to a short list of genuinely strong candidates rather than being forced there by the rule itself.

The 95 percent rule sits at the opposite end of the spectrum, useful mainly when an exchanger genuinely intends to acquire nearly everything named on the list, and it rarely overlaps in practice with a three-candidate strategy centered on naming a top choice plus two backups.

sections.heading: Deciding Which Rule to Use Before Day 45
sections.html: We make the call between the three-property rule and the alternatives once the candidate pipeline has developed enough to see which framework actually fits the deals on the table, not before the pipeline exists, since choosing the rule too early can mean structuring the sourcing effort around the wrong constraint.

faqs.q: Can more than three properties be identified under the three-property rule?
faqs.a: No. This rule caps the count at three named properties, with no restriction on their combined value. Naming a fourth property would require qualifying under a different identification rule instead.

faqs.q: Does the three-property rule work well for an exchanger who isn't sure which property they want yet?
faqs.a: It's riskier in that situation, since narrowing to only three names too early, before the pipeline has produced strong enough candidates, leaves little room if one or more falls through before closing.

faqs.q: Why would someone choose the three-property rule over the 200 percent rule?
faqs.a: Usually because the strongest candidate is worth more than twice the relinquished property's sale price, which the 200 percent rule's value cap would otherwise restrict, while the three-property rule imposes no value limit.

faqs.q: What happens if one of the three named properties falls out of contract after identification is filed?
faqs.a: The exchanger is generally limited to the remaining named properties unless a revocation and replacement is filed before the 45-day deadline itself passes. After that, no substitution is possible under this rule.

faqs.q: Is the three-property rule the default choice for most exchanges?
faqs.a: No, it's one of three available frameworks, and which one fits best depends on how many strong candidates exist and what their combined value looks like relative to the relinquished sale price.
